messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Rajesh

Rajesh was thirty-eight when he met Marcus at a gallery opening in Brooklyn. Marcus was charming, attentive, and seemed to understand the loneliness that had settled into Rajesh's life after his parents' death. For two years, their relationship felt like rescue. Then, during an argument about money in the spring of 2021, Marcus shoved him against the kitchen counter. The shock of it—the physical betrayal by someone Rajesh had allowed into his body and home—was less about pain than about the shattering of something Rajesh had believed was solid. Over the following months, the violence escalated. Marcus would grab him by the throat, pin him to walls, once threw a glass that cut Rajesh's shoulder. What made it worse was the pattern: Marcus would apologize, promise it would never happen again, and Rajesh would believe him because he wanted to, because the alternative—admitting he had failed at the one relationship he had fought so hard to build—felt impossible. When Rajesh finally left in December, he carried with him the certainty that he could not trust his own judgment. He had missed every warning sign. He had stayed too long. He had, by some logic his mind kept returning to, deserved it.

The first symptoms appeared within weeks. Rajesh found himself unable to sleep more than four hours a night, his body rigid in bed beside his new partner, Sarah, his mind cataloging exits and potential threats. When Sarah came home from work and called out his name in a voice slightly higher than usual, Rajesh's heart would race before his conscious mind had even registered what he'd heard. A client's raised voice during a design review would send a jolt through his nervous system so acute he'd excuse himself to the bathroom. By spring, he had begun to notice that certain sensory moments—the smell of whiskey on a colleague's breath, the sound of someone speaking rapid, slurred words that he couldn't quite parse—would trigger something immediate and overwhelming. His body would react first, flooding with adrenaline, his muscles tensing as though bracing for impact, before his rational mind could catch up and tell him he was safe in his office in Manhattan, that no one was about to hurt him. The incomprehensible chatter of drunk people on the subway, the acrid smell of alcohol wafting from a bar he passed on his commute, even the sensation of coming down with a cold—these ordinary moments had become dangerous, because each one carried him back to those moments with Marcus, the terror returning with photographic clarity. He could see Marcus's face above him, could feel the pressure of hands on his chest, could smell the whiskey on his breath, and the memory arrived not as a narrative but as a series of frozen images that his mind replayed with horrifying precision.

What terrified Rajesh most was not just the memories themselves but what they meant about him. He had come to believe that his inability to see Marcus's violence coming—his failure to recognize danger, his willingness to stay—revealed something fundamentally broken in his capacity to make sound decisions. When he felt ill, when his body began to register the early signs of flu, he would spiral into self-recrimination: *I can't trust myself to know what's real anymore.* The physical symptoms, the sensory triggers, they all fed back into his conviction that he was unreliable, that he had failed in the most important role of his life—to be a good partner, a discerning person, someone worthy of love. His body's hypervigilance, the way it would startle at the slightest unexpected sound, seemed to confirm his deepest fear: that he was damaged, that his threat detection had been broken all along, that perhaps it still was. And this belief—that he was fundamentally flawed—kept him awake at night, scanning the darkness for danger, unable to lower his guard because to do so felt like the same reckless trust that had nearly destroyed him.

Over the past year, Rajesh's avoidance had narrowed his world considerably. He stopped attending team dinners after work. He began requesting remote-only meetings, a request his firm accommodated but which marked him as difficult, unpredictable. Sarah noticed he would leave the room if she opened a bottle of wine. He could not sit in crowded bars or restaurants. The very architecture that had once brought him joy—designing open, collaborative spaces—now felt impossible to imagine inhabiting. He had come to therapy because Sarah had finally told him, with a firmness that cut through his fog, that she could not watch him disappear. What he wanted most was to trust again—to trust his instincts, his judgment, himself. What he feared most was that the person he had become—hypervigilant, doubtful, trapped in a loop of memory and threat—was permanent, that Marcus had rewritten something essential in him that could never be restored.
